title: Course map and assessment
summary: Turn the course outline into a study loop: data representation, scalable computation, and evaluation.
objectives: Separate lecture concepts from assignment deliverables

sections.title: Study lens
sections.body: For every algorithm, record the input model, the expensive pass over data, the memory bottleneck, and the failure mode.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Lecture and assignment material define the current study target; the MMDS index is attached as labeled depth, not merged into lecture scope.

contrastDrills.prompt: A dataset does not fit in memory. Which design assumption should you test first?
choices: Bound the working state and process incrementally
Ignore memory because Big-O is unchanged
contrastDrills.explanation: Streaming keeps a bounded summary and makes the number of passes explicit.

contrastDrills.prompt: When is an approximate count acceptable?
choices: When error is bounded and acceptable for the decision
Only when the dataset is tiny
contrastDrills.explanation: Approximation is a contract about error and decision risk, not a synonym for correctness.

math.explanation: Use this as a study model, not a universal theorem. A scalable algorithm tries to keep the number of full scans $p$ small and makes network movement and synchronization visible instead of hiding them inside a single runtime number.

symbols.meaning: number of passes over the data
time spent moving data between workers

math.caveat: The decomposition is a diagnostic lens; real runtimes also depend on skew, caching, serialization, and hardware.

criticalQuestions.prompt: If two implementations have the same Big-O time, which one would you choose for a dataset larger than main memory?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare passes, peak memory, network movement, skew, and recovery behavior rather than stopping at asymptotic notation.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A one-pass or streaming design may win because it avoids repeated reads and keeps the working set bounded, even when both methods have the same formal order.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What evidence would falsify the claim that an algorithm is scalable?
criticalQuestions.angle: Design a measurement that changes the input size, worker count, and partition distribution separately.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A flattening throughput curve, rapidly increasing shuffle time, or a single hot partition would contradict a simple scale-out claim.
